lead: At equilibrium, a liquid mixture and the vapour above it have fixed compositions at a given temperature and pressure. For an ideal binary mixture these compositions follow from the two pure-component vapour pressures and the total pressure. Distillation depends on this link: the vapour is richer in the more volatile component, so repeated vapour-liquid contacts separate the mixture. You use the same equilibrium relation to find whether a proposed separation is possible, to size flash drums, and to step stages on a y-x diagram.
prereq: You need: basic mole fraction and Dalton's law from chemistry; nothing from Unit 1 is needed, and 4.2 uses this equilibrium directly.

blocks.text: Take a binary mixture of A and B. Mole fraction x<sub>A</sub> is moles of A in the liquid divided by total moles in the liquid; y<sub>A</sub> is the same in the vapour. P is total pressure. P°<sub>A</sub> and P°<sub>B</sub> are the vapour pressures of pure A and pure B at the same temperature. Some syllabi call this vapour-liquid equilibrium (VLE).
p<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>;  P = p<sub>A</sub> + p<sub>B</sub>
blocks.where: p<sub>A</sub> is the partial pressure of A (kPa); x<sub>A</sub> is liquid mole fraction; P°<sub>A</sub> is pure-A vapour pressure at the same temperature (kPa); P is total pressure (kPa).

blocks.text: Raoult's law gives p<sub>A</sub> from the liquid composition. Dalton's law adds the two partial pressures. Combine them for B as p<sub>B</sub> = (1 − x<sub>A</sub>)P°<sub>B</sub>, then solve for x<sub>A</sub>. The result is the bubble-point equation: a liquid of composition x<sub>A</sub> starts to boil at pressure P when the temperature makes the two P° values satisfy it. The vapour composition follows from y<sub>A</sub> = p<sub>A</sub>/P.
x<sub>A</sub> = (P − P°<sub>B</sub>)/(P°<sub>A</sub> − P°<sub>B</sub>);  y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>/P
blocks.where: x<sub>A</sub> is liquid mole fraction of A; y<sub>A</sub> is vapour mole fraction of A; P is total pressure (kPa); P°<sub>A</sub> and P°<sub>B</sub> are pure-component vapour pressures (kPa).

blocks.text: For a two-phase mixture, P must lie between P°<sub>B</sub> and P°<sub>A</sub> when A is the more volatile component. If P is greater than P°<sub>A</sub>, the mixture is all liquid. If P is less than P°<sub>B</sub>, it is all vapour. In design you use the liquid x to get the equilibrium y. Raoult's law uses x, not y.

sections.h3: Relative volatility and the y-x curve

blocks.text: Relative volatility α<sub>AB</sub> measures how easily A leaves B. It is the ratio of the vapour-to-liquid ratios of the two components. For an ideal mixture obeying Raoult's law, the pressure ratios simplify to the ratio of pure-component vapour pressures.

blocks.where: α<sub>AB</sub> is relative volatility of A with respect to B (dimensionless); y<sub>A</sub>, y<sub>B</sub> are vapour mole fractions; x<sub>A</sub>, x<sub>B</sub> are liquid mole fractions; P°<sub>A</sub>, P°<sub>B</sub> are pure-component vapour pressures at the same temperature (kPa).

blocks.text: If α > 1, A is more volatile and the vapour is richer in A. Rearranging the definition gives yA = α xA/[1 + (α − 1)xA]. For α = 3, the equilibrium curve starts at (0,0), passes through (0.5,0.75), and ends at (1,1). It lies above the diagonal y = x. The gap between the curve and the diagonal is the driving force for separation. On a y-x diagram, horizontal and vertical steps between this curve and an operating line give theoretical stages (see 4.4). On a T-x-y diagram at fixed P, the lower curve is the bubble-point line and the upper curve is the dew-point line; the area between them is two-phase. A more volatile component has a lower boiling point and a higher y.

Real mixtures depart from Raoult's law because liquid interactions are not ideal. A simple correction is p<sub>A</sub> = γ<sub>A</sub> x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>, where γ<sub>A</sub> is the activity coefficient; γ<sub>A</sub> = 1 for an ideal solution. Predicting γ<sub>A</sub> from models belongs to thermodynamics, not to this chapter.

A real y-x curve can cross the diagonal. At the crossing point xA = yA and α = 1. That composition is an azeotrope. At an azeotrope the vapour and liquid have the same composition, so ordinary distillation cannot pass it; a separating agent is needed (see 4.9). Common examples are the minimum-boiling ethanol-water azeotrope and the maximum-boiling nitric acid-water azeotrope.

For real systems, α changes with x, especially near an azeotrope. Use measured VLE for design when the mixture is non-ideal; treat Raoult's law as a starting estimate for similar components. These same equations support flash calculations in 4.2, where a feed is partly vaporised and the equilibrium gives the vapour and liquid products.

examples.question: A binary ideal mixture has P°<sub>A</sub> = 120 kPa and P°<sub>B</sub> = 40 kPa at the column pressure P = 101.3 kPa. Find the equilibrium liquid mole fraction x<sub>A</sub>, vapour mole fraction y<sub>A</sub>, and relative volatility α.
steps: Write the data: P = 101.3 kPa, P°<sub>A</sub> = 120 kPa, P°<sub>B</sub> = 40 kPa.
Use the bubble-point equation: x<sub>A</sub> = (101.3 − 40)/(120 − 40) = 61.3/80 = 0.76625, which rounds to 0.766.
Find the vapour composition: y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>/P = 0.76625 × 120/101.3 = 91.95/101.3 = 0.9077, which rounds to 0.908.
examples.answer: At P = 101.3 kPa, x<sub>A</sub> = 0.766, y<sub>A</sub> = 0.908, and α = 3.0.
examples.check:
P_A = 120.0
P_B = 40.0
P = 101.3
x_A = (P - P_B)/(P_A - P_B)
y_A = x_A*P_A/P
alpha = P_A/P_B
print(round(x_A, 3))
print(round(y_A, 3))
print(round(alpha, 1))

traps: Mixing x and y: Raoult's law uses liquid x; vapour y comes out of y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>/P.
Using P° values at a different temperature: both pure-component vapour pressures must be at the equilibrium temperature.
Calling α constant for real mixtures: α changes with x, and α = 1 at an azeotrope.
Forgetting the pressure condition: the bubble-point equation needs P between P°<sub>B</sub> and P°<sub>A</sub> for a two-phase mixture when A is more volatile.
Using mass fraction in place of mole fraction: all VLE equations here use mole fractions.

quiz.q: Define x<sub>A</sub> and y<sub>A</sub> for a binary mixture.
quiz.a: x<sub>A</sub> is moles of A in the liquid divided by total moles in the liquid. y<sub>A</sub> is moles of A in the vapour divided by total moles in the vapour.

quiz.q: Why is y<sub>A</sub> greater than x<sub>A</sub> when α > 1?
quiz.a: α > 1 means A is more volatile than B, so the vapour is enriched in A. The equilibrium curve y<sub>A</sub> against x<sub>A</sub> lies above the diagonal y = x.

quiz.q: An ideal mixture has P°<sub>A</sub> = 100 kPa, P°<sub>B</sub> = 50 kPa, and P = 80 kPa. Find x<sub>A</sub>, y<sub>A</sub>, and α.
A mixture has α = 1 at a certain composition. What does this mean for ordinary distillation?
quiz.a: At α = 1 the vapour and liquid compositions are equal. That is an azeotrope, and ordinary distillation cannot change the composition past it.

quiz.q: Write Raoult's law and Dalton's law for a binary mixture.
quiz.a: Raoult's law: p<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub> and p<sub>B</sub> = x<sub>B</sub> P°<sub>B</sub>. Dalton's law: P = p<sub>A</sub> + p<sub>B</sub>.

quiz.q: Why must Raoult's law use x, not y?
quiz.a: Raoult's law predicts the partial pressure above a liquid from the liquid composition. The vapour composition is a result: y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P°<sub>A</sub>/P.

quiz.q: For α = 2.5 and x<sub>A</sub> = 0.4, find y<sub>A</sub>.
On a T-x-y diagram at fixed pressure, what is the state above the dew-point curve and below the bubble-point curve?
quiz.a: Above the dew-point curve the mixture is all vapour. Below the bubble-point curve it is all liquid. Between the two curves it is a two-phase liquid-vapour mixture.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial VLE data come from measured pressure-temperature-composition experiments and are fitted with activity-coefficient or equation-of-state models. Process simulators store such data and interpolate equilibrium for column design. Search terms: PTx data, NRTL, UNIQUAC, UNIFAC, azeotrope search. Newer curricula add COSMO-based predictions and machine-learning VLE surrogates.
